Overview

Figurines were made for various reasons and were often accessible to many people. These differently shaped bodies are votive offerings or amulets used for protection, ensuring health and/or fertility, invoking the divine, or for afterlife beliefs. These are an important reflection of the reality of diversity, rather than an ‘ideal’ body.  

The Objects

2 Reclining Figure View

2 Reclining Figure, MU4249, front view © Gale History Museum

Alt text: Object 2. Reclining figure. This mould-made ceramic figure depicts a person reclining on their left side on a chaise-like base. The bodily and facial features are unclear due to the softness of the moulding. Remnants of pink-red, cream, and yellow paint are heavily worn on the base, back, and legs of the figure.
3 Bronze dancer (replica) View

3 Bronze dancer, MU0101, front view © Gale History Museum

Alt text: Object 3. Bronze dancer (a replica), a metal figurine of a woman appearing to dance, fitted to a wooden base.
4 Figure of a musician View

4. Figure of a musician, MU0086, front view © Gale History Museum

Alt text: Object 4. Figure of a Musician. A carved figure kneeling, holding a drum with both hands.
5 Seated statuette View

5. Seated statuette, MU3735, front view © Gale History Museum

Alt text: Object 5. Seated statuette. A ceramic statuette of a seated human figure. The object is possibly mould-made and is placed on a (modern) black base. The figure wears a large and tall circular headdress and is seated upright.
6 Bronze figure of Priapus View

Bronze figure of Priapus, MU4697, front view © Gale History Museum

Alt text: Object 6. Bronze figure of Priapus. A metal figurine of the deity Priapus. He is facing forward with an obviously enlarged and erect penis.
7 Terracotta figurine View

Terracotta figurine, MU2676, front view © Gale History Museum

Alt text: Object 7. Terracotta figurine, a ceramic human-like figure. The face is shaped with a long, pointed nose, and holes in the clay indicate eyes and a mouth. The body is very loosely moulded and flares widely to a circular shape at the bottom. The figure is placed on a black (modern) square base.
8 Amulet of Pataikos View

Amulet of Pataikos, MU0523, front view © Gale History Museum

Alt text: Object 8. Amulet of Pataikos. Moulded in faience, a teal-green glazed ceramic, this small amuletic figure is of the ancient Egyptian deity Pataikos. Represented as a standing male figure with dwarfism, a large head, and clenched fists, with legs slightly bent apart. Behind the figure's head, there is a loop for it to be worn.
